steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The lighthouse had no name on any map, but in the logbooks it was always written the same way: North Spire, occupied.

Occupied meant Ezra.

He had been there for fourteen years, three months, and five days. He knew because the tally was carved into the underside of his bunk, where the wood was smooth from his thumb tracing it that first sleepless month, then the next, then the next, until solitude itself became a kind of weather he no longer remarked on.

On most days, the routine kept the world in order. Wake with the dull gray of dawn, stoke the old iron stove, grind coffee beans in the chipped hand-mill. Downstairs, check the oil levels, inspect the prisms of the Fresnel lens for dust or salt, polish the brass rails until the metal shone like a second sunrise.

By midmorning the fog would roll in, as soft and impenetrable as wool. The horn would mournfully sound its measured note into the blankness, and Ezra would walk the circular stairs, inspecting for leaks in the stone, for hairline cracks, for anything that could betray the lighthouse’s single sacred obligation: to stand and to warn.

There was comfort in the constancy of it. Ships came and went beyond the pale curtain of mist. He saw their lights, heard their engines, plotted their positions in his log with the tiny, sure strokes of someone who is both witness and secret-keeper. The world moved, and the lamp turned, and Ezra remained.

Only at night, when the light was at its brightest and the black sea leaned in with its endless hush, did he sometimes feel the old question pressing against his ribs: Why stay?

The answer was both simple and impossible to articulate. Once, there had been another keeper, Agnes. She had trained him, shown him how to coax the balky generators into life, how to anticipate storms from the taste of the air. In those days, the nights had been shaped by her stories, her laugh, the chessboard permanently set up on the kitchen table.

Then the budget cuts came, and the Service offered relocation. They would shutter North Spire. Automation, they said. Satellites. GPS. No need for lonely stones lashed by centuries of weather.

Agnes took the transfer inland. Ezra surprised them all—including himself—by refusing.

He stayed when the supply boats were reduced, when the paint peeled in ragged strips from the railing, when the brass plate by the door listing the names of past keepers grew dulled by salt and neglect. He stayed as the forms on his yearly reports changed from “Lighthouse Keeper” to “Contracted Maintenance.”

He stayed because he had lived enough of his life in crowded rooms and restless cities to know that the quiet here was not emptiness but depth. Because a boyhood shipwreck—his father’s fishing boat, a night without a lighthouse in sight—had left him with the understanding that some absences could be fatal.

So he remained, and kept the light.

•

The storm came on a Tuesday, which Ezra disliked on principle. Storms, in his mind, belonged to weekends, to days with names that could carry their weight. But this one slid in under the flat banner of an ordinary weekday and swelled into something enormous before the barometer quite believed it.

By afternoon the horizon had vanished. The sky was greenish, bruise-colored, the kind of color that made animals go quiet. Ezra moved through his checklist with more than usual care, tightening down every latch, double-securing windows, checking that the backup generator coughed obediently to life. On the sea, waves were already knotting themselves into higher and stranger shapes.

He radioed the harbormaster on the mainland.

“North Spire to Port Haven. You seeing this, Thom?”

The reply crackled, half-eaten by static. “We see it. Forecast says it’ll blow over by midnight.”

“Forecast is lying,” Ezra said, eyeing the low, fast clouds.

There was a pause, then Thom’s dry chuckle. “It usually is. Keep her burning, Ez.”

“Always.”

Night fell early, or perhaps it merely folded into the storm. The lighthouse’s beam cut a clean, revolving arc through the thrashing darkness. Rain hurled itself against the glass in sheets. Outside, the air was full of the kind of roar that left no room for smaller sounds, an unbroken animal bellow of wind and water crashing themselves to pieces against stone.

Ezra rode it the way a captain rides out rough seas: moving steadily, never rushing but never idle. Up and down the steps, checking the lamp, checking the generator, checking the old mortar between the stones for seepage. Each circuit ended with a brief stop by the long window that faced east, where the beam swung out to rake the horizon.

Hours into the storm, during one of these pauses, he saw it.

At first it was just something wrong in the rhythm. The lighthouse beam turned with reliable grace, but far beyond its reach there was a flicker, then another, jagged and unreliable. Ezra narrowed his eyes, pressing his forehead to the cool glass to cut the interior reflections.

There: a small, frantic light, winking in the wild black. Not the steady white or red of a navigation buoy, not the sweeping wash of another lighthouse. A handheld light, then lost behind a wave, then stabbing upward again.

Morse, he realized a moment later. It was trying to be Morse, though the sea kept stealing half the letters.

… — S O S …

The old language flared inside him like a second heart. Agnes had insisted he learn it on real brass keys, slamming out dots and dashes until they were muscle memory. Useless skill, some had said even then. Obsolete. And yet here it was, knocking at his window.

Ezra grabbed his binoculars. The glass was rain-smeared, and the world beyond it was a mad smear of gray and black, but after a few searching passes he found them: a small boat, no bigger than a lifeboat, heaving like a cork. Its bow would rear up, vanish in spray, then plunge, leaving only the pale oval of a face visible against the dark.

The light was a flare gun, he realized, fired and now being shaken by whoever held it as though sheer desperation could keep it burning. Each time it dipped behind a wall of water his fist tightened on the binoculars.

There was no question of launching his own boat; even at the thought, he barked a humorless laugh. North Spire’s narrow landing was a death sentence in these conditions. The only meaningful thing he could do was the one thing that was already his occupation.

He could keep the light.

And yet staying inside the tower while someone fought for their life out there felt like a crime.

He yanked the radio from its mount. “North Spire to Port Haven. Vessel in distress east-northeast of my position, approximate bearing zero-eight-five. Small craft, no running lights. They’re firing flares. Storm conditions severe, repeat, severe. Over.”

Static. A burst, then Thom’s strained voice: “Copy that, North Spire. Patrol is grounded. Coast Guard cutter still two hours out, and that’s if the sea shows mercy. Mark their position if you can. Hold that light, Ezra.”

As if he needed telling.

He killed the cabin lights to give his eyes more dark. Up in the lantern room, under the great domed glass, the heart of the lighthouse turned with its stately, indifferent precision. Ezra moved like a shadow around its base, adjusting the shutters to widen the beam’s sweep, focusing more brightness on the quadrant where the boat struggled.

The storm breathed and roared. The lighthouse answered with its single slow phrase of light, turning and turning, casting its white arm over the drowning world.

Between sweeps, Ezra could not see the boat at all. Each time the beam returned to that slice of ocean he searched for that frantic spark. Once, twice, three times the light came up empty, striking only on the shattered white of wave-crests. His stomach crawled.

On the fourth rotation, just as the beam skimmed the horizon, the flare winked back, weak but undeniable. Closer to the rocks now. Far too close.

“Come on,” he whispered, as if the boat could hear him. “See me. See me.”

The beam swept over them, and, in his mind’s eye, he traced its path straight into whoever’s eyes were out there—cold, stinging, desperate—hoping they would understand what that light meant. Not salvation, not certainly; just the information that the world had not entirely forgotten them. That here was a warning: rocks below, death if you come closer. Deep water safer, if you can reach it.

The wind slammed itself against the lighthouse with a force that made the glass groan. Somewhere below, a shutter tore loose and flapped open, banging a feral counterpoint. Ezra flinched but did not leave his post. His hands had found the metal railing around the lamp and were clenched white on it, as though he were holding the whole tower steady through sheer stubbornness.

Time lost its edges. There was only the turning of the light, the intermittent, maddening glimpses of that tiny battling craft, the unceasing roar. Now and then he would dive down the spiral, slam the radio button, bark updates to Port Haven. “They’re still up.” “They’ve drifted north.” “They’re too damned close to the teeth.”

Once, between transmissions, Thom’s voice came back, oddly gentle. “It’s not on you if—”

Ezra cut him off. “Not the time.”

Because if there was any space in his mind for that thought, it would ram itself straight into the question he had been carefully ignoring for fourteen years: what, exactly, did it mean that he had built his life around preventing other people’s catastrophes? How many had slipped past anyway in the nights when the fog was too thick or the sea too cruel?

He could not afford that circuitry now. There was only the beam. Only the choice to keep it unwavering.

At some point—how long after he first saw the flare, he would never be sure—the storm began to tire. Its howls pitched lower, its fury became more intermittent. The waves were still monstrous, but their crests shredded more, their blows against the rock less concussive.

In the thinning rain, Ezra picked out a new set of lights to the north: the heavy, steady lamps of the Coast Guard cutter, nosing its way toward the coordinates he’d relayed. Between its sweeps and his own, the ocean around the small boat was suddenly full of light, as if two great arms were rummaging through the wreckage of the storm, refusing to let it hide what it had tried to claim.

He watched the dance with a breathless, useless intensity: the cutter’s searchlights finding the tossing dot of the lifeboat, the momentary tangle as ropes were thrown and missed, thrown and caught. There was a long, terrible minute when the lifeboat disappeared entirely from both beams and his heart jackhammered against his ribs. Then—there. Closer to the cutter now, half-swallowed in its lee.

His throat hurt. He realized he was whispering the old numerals under his breath: counting seconds in arcs of the beam, as if he could push time along faster by naming it.

At last, like a magician concluding a trick, the cutter drew the lifeboat in and the flickering little light vanished against its hulking side. There would be more to it—the hauling of bodies over railings, the brutal tenderness of resuscitation—but from where he stood, high and salt-battered, this was as much as he would see.

He kept the lighthouse burning anyway, all through the slow, sodden withdrawal of the storm, through the cutter’s cautious retreat toward the safety of the harbor. Only when its lights were small as stars did he let himself sit on the iron stair, elbows on his knees, and drop his head into his hands.

He sat that way until the gray of dawn began to seep into the world, until the automatic timer sighed and began the mechanism to shutter the lamp. Ezra rose, muscles complaining, and went through the rituals of shutting down: checking the fuel, recording the night’s events in the logbook in a tight, precise hand.

Under “Notes” he paused for a moment, pen hovering, then wrote:

“2310 hrs: Observed distress flares from unidentified small craft. Maintained full luminous intensity. Coordinates relayed to Port Haven and CG. 0054 hrs: CG cutter reported successful retrieval of survivors. Lamp functioned without interruption.”

He stared at that last sentence for a while. Lamp functioned without interruption. As if that were the whole story.

After breakfast, exhausted but restless, he climbed out onto the narrow maintenance ledge that circled the lantern room. The wind had faded to a stiff breeze; the sea, though still smeared with long, sullen swells, was beginning to glitter again under a watery sun. In the distance, the mainland was a low smudge. Somewhere over there, in a harbor medical ward, people who had last night been certain they were going to die would be waking up under fluorescent lights, baffled, grateful, angry, or all three at once.

He imagined them being told, by some harried officer, that a lighthouse had seen them. It occurred to him that for many of them, he would be a story at best, or a detail they’d soon forget. “The lighthouse spotted your flares.” Not the keeper. Not Ezra.

He ran his palm over the rough stone of the outer wall, feeling where the wind had eaten at it over the years, softening edges. His fingers brushed the old brass nameplate by the door as he went back inside, the one dulled nearly to illegibility. He scraped away some salt with his thumbnail until the letters caught the sun again.

North Spire Light.

Below that, if you squinted, you could still see the ghost of smaller letters: Agnes Roe, Keeper. A diagonal scratch ran through the name, left by some careless cargo years ago. Ezra had never polished it out. It seemed wrong to erase even a wound.

He went downstairs. There was a chessboard on the kitchen table, dusty but undisturbed, an old game frozen mid-strategy.

He set a kettle on. While it hummed, he found the small wooden box at the back of the cupboard and opened it, lifting out the brass Morse key. Its surface was worn smooth by decades of fingers, Agnes’s first and then his. Technology had rendered it museum-worthy years ago. Still, the Service had never asked for it back.

On impulse, he plugged it into the compact radio and tuned the frequency to the channel used by harbor traffic. Rules or no rules, someone would be listening. His hand hovered over the key.

Transmitting was not his job anymore. They had automated beacons, computerized systems issuing perfect, neutral reports. The human voice, the human hand tapping imperfect, emotional messages into the ether, that was meant to be over.

But last night’s flare-light still burned at the back of his eyelids. The way it had insisted on being seen. On existing. On meaning.

He pressed the key down. The small machine answered with a clean, crisp click.

He sent: N O R T H   S P I R E   O C C U P I E D.

The pattern flowed through him like an old song. It went out into the air, over the water.

There was a pause. Then, to his surprise, an answering cascade of clicks came trickling back. His lips twitched.

Understood, the message said, in Thom’s slightly clumsy hand. Still needed.

Ezra sat for a long moment, hand resting lightly on the key, not pressing, not yet sending anything back. Outside, gulls were beginning to circle, arguing over driftwood and secrets the storm had thrown ashore. The sea, as it always did, pretended nothing had happened.

Eventually, he rose. There was brass to polish, glass to clean, a lens to inspect. By sunset, the light would need to be perfect again.

He moved back into his routine, but something in its center had shifted. It was as if, in the turning of his own beam over the lives of others, he had briefly seen his own path lit from afar—a solitary figure on a stone tower, waving a lamp against the dark, answering a question no one had thought to stop asking.

The world would continue to crowd itself with newer, smaller, smarter lights. Systems would improve; budgets would tighten again. One day, perhaps, North Spire’s great lamp would be powered down for the last time.

But not yet.

Tonight, somewhere beyond the curve of the world, a sailor would look up from a wet deck, or a passenger would lift a fogged airplane windowshade, and see a pulse of white turning in a measured rhythm. They might not know its name. They would likely never think of the man climbing the spiral staircase inside it, checking oil levels, watching weather, answering flares.

Still, the light would be there.

Occupied, the logbooks would say.

Occupied, and keeping watch.
